Mention another volume only when it shares the same instance EBS baseline, and then as a Separate finding. Leave out AWS FIS experiments, AWS CloudTrail events and alarms on resources that are not attached to the instance.\\\\n- Link a gap only to the findings it affects. Each proposal also gives the exact AWS CLI command the customer can run with their own credentials. See [Change proposals](references/finding-logic.md#change-proposals).\\\\n- **Deletes are manual customer steps.** AWS DevOps Agent refuses delete-class operations (for example DeleteSnapshot, DeleteVolume, DeregisterImage), so never propose them as directed actions. Do not end the turn with a question tool or a request to pick a value: give the recommended proposal, and the command for any value the user named, then say the user can choose.\\\\n- **Discover, don\\'t assume:** read every configuration value from the APIs.\\\\n- **Given facts stay given.** When the user supplies the values and asks you to treat them as given, reason from those values only. State this rule in the answer whenever a modification is in progress or proposed.\\\\n- **No interpretation without data:** report what couldn\\'t be checked and use fallbacks. `DescribeVolumesModifications` returns only the most recent modification per volume; modification history and counts come from the optional AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` events, or are listed under Gaps.\\\\n- **Units:** MiB/s for throughput, stated every time.\\\\n- **Escalate** on scope signals or when the investigation can\\'t explain the symptom.\\\\n\\\\n## Gotchas\\\\n\\\\n- A modification in `optimizing` is not stuck. The new size, IOPS or throughput already applies while it optimizes.\\\\n- `DescribeInstanceTypes` reports EBS bandwidth in MB/s. Convert it to MiB/s before comparing it with volume throughput.\\\\n- On io1 and io2, `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is the percentage of provisioned IOPS delivered. Run each area per Region, rate each finding with the scale in [finding-logic.md](finding-logic.md), and write the report with [review-report-format.md](review-report-format.md).\\n\\nThe Capacity and quota headroom section is also a shared capability. Troubleshoot paths use it when an operation failed on a limit.\\n\\n## Capacity and quota headroom\\n\\n**Checks**\\n\\nRun every check below even when the error looks simple. A user who reports a quota error has already failed to fix it alone, so give documented findings in the verdict format, not a short chat reply. Whether the run is a chat or a formal investigation is decided by how the user starts it, not by this skill.\\n\\n1. If an operation failed, quote the error and name the quota it refers to. For example \"You have exceeded your maximum io2 IOPS limit of 100000 IOPS in this region\" refers to the regional io2 IOPS quota, which is separate from the per-volume maximum.\\n2. `ListServiceQuotas --service-code ebs`: quota name, code, applied `Value`, `Adjustable`. Use measured values and the limits read from the APIs. Do not use fixed percentage triggers.\\n\\n1. Is `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` or `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` at 1, is the summed IOPS or MiB/s of all attached volumes flat at the instance EBS baseline, or are `EBSIOBalance%` / `EBSByteBalance%` draining or at 0?\\n   - Yes: **Instance**. Say \"the volume has headroom; raising volume IOPS will not help; change the instance type\". If a volume is also flat at its own limit, report both and fix the instance first, because volume changes cannot deliver above the instance ceiling.\\n2. Is the instance healthy and one volume flat at its own provisioned limit on the dimension its type is judged by, or is its `VolumeIOPSExceededCheck` or `VolumeThroughputExceededCheck` at 1?\\n   - Yes: **Volume**.\\n3. Is a gp2, st1 or sc1 volume\\'s `BurstBalance` draining or at 0?\\n   - Yes: **Burst credits**.\\n4. Did an operation fail on a quota (error text names a limit)?\\n   - Yes: **Quota**. Use the Capacity and quota headroom section of [review-operational.md](review-operational.md).\\n5. Are all layers below their limits, latency at the volume\\'s normal level, and queue length low?\\n   - Yes: **Not EBS**. Check CPU, memory, network and the application.\\n6. Are all layers below their limits, with the four exceeded checks at 0, but latency and `VolumeQueueLength` up while IOPS and throughput collapse? Check for a direct signal:\\n   - `VolumeStalledIOCheck` failed (value 1) for the volume, or\\n   - `DescribeVolumeStatus` reports the volume as impaired or a status check as failed, or\\n   - an open AWS Health event for the volume, its Availability Zone or its Region.\\n\\n   Then decide:\\n   - A running AWS FIS experiment targets the volume or instance: the latency is injected. Say so plainly; it ends with the experiment (see Step 5 of [troubleshoot-performance.md](troubleshoot-performance.md)). Never recommend more provisioning.\\n   - One or more direct signals: **AWS-side impairment**. Never recommend more provisioning. Follow the escalation rules below.\\n   - No direct signal and no FIS experiment: **Indeterminate**. Keep the cause open. Do not name AWS-side impairment and do not recommend more provisioning. Present the candidate causes as described in the next section. Tell the customer to check the AWS Health Dashboard for an ongoing AWS-side issue and to watch the volume status checks and `VolumeStalledIOCheck`. If the symptom persists, follow the escalation rules below.\\n\\n## Indeterminate: candidate causes\\n\\nAn Indeterminate verdict is a short list of candidate causes, not a single sentence. The Binding layer stays Indeterminate, and the answer says so in those words: \"Binding layer: Indeterminate\".\\n\\nStart with the answer to the user\\'s question and the reason, for example \"Binding layer: Indeterminate. Adding IOPS will not help: the volume uses 15 percent of its provisioned IOPS and 16 percent of its throughput, and the four exceeded checks are 0.\" Then give the candidates. For each candidate give:\\n\\n- a title that matches what the data shows (for a cause the data rules out, say so in the title, for example \"Volume or instance limit: ruled out\"),\\n- the supporting observations, with numbers derived from the measured or given values,\\n- the specific check that would confirm it or rule it out, and its result if you ran it.\\n\\nKeep the list short and specific:\\n\\n- List only the candidates that fit the volume type and the data, most likely first. Burst credits apply to gp2, st1 and sc1, not to gp3 or io2.\\n- Merge candidates that overlap. Each candidate needs its own observations and its own check; if two would share them, they are one candidate.\\n- Put candidates that the data makes unlikely (for example sub-minute bursts when the exceeded checks are 0) in the ruled-out candidate with the numbers, instead of listing each one on its own.\\n- Describe the pattern in plain terms (\"latency and queue length rose while IOPS fell, below every limit\"). Do not call it an impairment pattern, because without a direct signal it is not one.\\n\\nUseful derived numbers for the observations:\\n\\n- Percentage of each limit in use (measured IOPS and MiB/s against the volume and the instance limits).\\n- Time per I/O from queue length and IOPS (Little\\'s law): time per I/O in ms = average queue length / IOPS x 1,000. When the queue value is not known, give the time each unit of queue adds at the measured IOPS (for example \"at 900 IOPS, each 1.0 of queue length adds about 1.1 ms\"). A queue that grows while IOPS falls means each I/O takes longer, not that a rate limit was reached.\\n- Average I/O size = throughput / IOPS, compared with the 256 KiB maximum I/O size that SSD volumes count as one operation (larger I/O is split into 256 KiB operations). Recheck while the symptom lasts. If it persists with all checks clean, escalate to AWS Support with the evidence pack |\\n| Injected latency from a fault injection experiment | AWS FIS `ListExperiments` for a running experiment with `aws:ebs:volume-io-latency` or `aws:ebs:pause-volume-io` that targets the volume or instance |\\n| A change in the workload\\'s I/O pattern (larger I/O, more random I/O, more writes) | Average I/O size and the read and write split before and during the alarm window, from `VolumeReadBytes`, `VolumeWriteBytes`, `VolumeReadOps` and `VolumeWriteOps` |\\n| The instance EBS limit, shared with the other attached volumes | Summed IOPS and MiB/s of every attached volume, including the root volume, against the `DescribeInstanceTypes` baseline; `InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck` and `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck`; `EBSIOBalance%` and `EBSByteBalance%` |\\n| A cause outside Amazon EBS on the instance (application locks, file system, CPU) | `CPUUtilization` and the attribution matrix below. OS-level data such as `iostat` is outside this skill, so ask the customer for it |\\n| Volume initialization after a restore from a snapshot | `DescribeVolumes` `SnapshotId` and `CreateTime` |\\n| Volume or instance limit, including sub-minute bursts | The limits table and the four exceeded checks. Adding IOPS will not help\", and its description gives the reason with the numbers, the clean direct signals, what to watch and when to escalate.\\n- Each candidate is its own finding. Link to it the observations that support it or rule it out, so each one shows its supporting observations.\\n- Link a gap only to the candidates it affects. A gap that applies to everything (for example \"the values were given by the user, not read from the APIs\") is recorded once and not repeated under every candidate.\\n\\nWhen the user gives the values and asks you to treat them as given, build the candidates from those values only. Do not query the account for other resources and do not mix account data into the given facts. List under Gaps that the values were not read from the APIs. Describe the impact from the given values (percent of each limit in use, time each unit of queue adds, average I/O size) instead of writing that it is unknown.\\n\\n### Qualitative attribution matrix for \"is it storage?\"\\n\\nFrom the attribution draft, with the numeric CPU bands removed because no public source states them.\\n\\n| CPU | Volume latency | Queue length | Likely attribution |\\n|---|---|---|---|\\n| High | High | High | Application drives heavy I/O. Both compute and storage are stressed |\\n| High | Normal | Low | Compute, not storage |\\n| Low | High | High | Storage. The application waits on I/O. Go to the decision tree |\\n| Low | Normal | Low | Neither. Check network, locks and the application |\\n\\n\"High\" and \"normal\" mean compared with the same resource\\'s own history and the type\\'s documented expectation in [metrics-thresholds.md](metrics-thresholds.md).\\n\\n## Change proposals\\n\\nEvery mutating change (`ModifyVolume`, an AWS KMS key or key policy change, a quota request, an instance type change) is a proposal. Include all of these:\\n\\n1. **Whether the change will help,** from the measured data. If the data shows it will not help, say so first and say what will.\\n2. **The exact call,** as an AWS CLI command with every parameter filled in from the APIs, for example `aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id <volume-id> --iops <target> --region <region>`. If a different value is better (for example the instance EBS baseline caps what the volume can deliver), also give the command for the recommended value and how it was computed.\\n3. **Expected effect,** including the next limit (for example \"the instance baseline of `<n>` IOPS then caps delivered IOPS\").\\n4. **For a volume modification:** the state sequence (`modifying`, `optimizing`, `completed`), the rule of up to 4 modifications per volume in a rolling 24-hour window with each one completing before the next, and how many remain after this change from the AWS CloudTrail `ModifyVolume` count (or say the count is unconfirmed and list it under Gaps).\\n5. **Rollback,** as the exact reverse command and when it is possible (after the change completes for a volume, and it counts toward the 4; size cannot be reduced).\\n6. **Cost direction,** with a link to the pricing page. This change runs only as a directed action that an operator approves on the approval card.\" If directed actions are not available in this Agent Space, say so and say that the customer can run the command above with their own credentials.\\n\\nDelete-class operations are never directed actions.
